newsitem.title: USA: UPS, striking Teamsters set to resume talks.
newsitem.headline: UPS, striking Teamsters set to resume talks.

text.p: The Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service headed back to the bargaining table on Thursday, but with few hopes of ending the strike that has crippled the nation's largest package delivery company.

"I think it's very important that we not have unrealistic expectations," said John Calhoun Wells, the federal mediator who brought the two sides back together for the meeting. "These are very very difficult issues on the table."

All the two sides seemed to agree on ahead of the 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) meeting was that there was little to negotiate. With the strike in its fourth day, the parties face unresolved issues, including pay and benefits, the company's use of part-time workers and pensions.
UPS -- which normally handles 12 million packages a day -- reiterated it would agree to no major changes to its last proposal, offered before the strike began.
"UPS remains committed to its final contract offer and is encouraging the union leaders to let UPS Teamsters vote on the proposal," the company said in a statement.
Teamster President Ron Carey said that if UPS was unwilling to negotiate big changes to its offer, there could be no contract.
"We have seen no sign that the company has changed its attitude, so we are not particularly optimistic about these new talks," Carey said late on Wednesday.
Wells said Carey and UPS negotiator Dave Murray were sitting down without any expectation of a quick deal.
"This is the kind of meeting where we ask people to check their guns at the door, sit down and make peace," he told reporters. "It is not a formal bargaining session."
The announcement that talks would resume was welcomed by businesses, which face headaches moving packages and higher shipping costs from overloaded UPS rivals.
The strike by 185,000 Teamsters began at a minute past midnight EDT on Monday (0401 GMT) after a last-ditch 17-hour marathon negotiation collapsed.
The Teamsters blamed the strike on the company's refusal to create thousands of full-time jobs each year from part-time positions and to stop handing union work to outside suppliers.
Between 120,000 and 130,000 union-represented workers are part-time. The union represents about two-thirds of the 300,000 worker Atlanta-based company.

UPS called those issues "a smoke screen," saying the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms. UPS says running its own pension plan would save it money in the long run.

Since the strike began, UPS has been handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments, using 50,000 non-union employees to do the work of striking loaders, sorters and drivers. The company said more than 97 percent of the Teamsters were staying away from work.
The two sides agreed to meet after days of pressure from the Clinton administration, though the White House has resisted calls to step in and end the strike.
Business leaders warned that there would be massive layoffs at small- and mid-size firms struggling to move their goods if the strikers were not ordered back to work.

But President Clinton told a White House news conference on Wednesday he could only intervene by invoking the Taft-Hartley Law, which authorises the president to halt strikes that threaten the nation's safety or economic health.
"There has to be a severe damage to the country. The test is ... very high before the president can intervene," he said.

One news report said the Department of Transportation had prepared a study on economic damage from the strike. A Transportation spokesman declined to confirm or deny the report, except to say the department was closely monitoring the economic effects of the strike.
